slides.0.title: Winemaking I: pressing, first fermentation and blending
slides.0.subtitle: From whole bunches to a blended base wine
slides.1.title: Pressing: cuvée and taille
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Whole bunch, gentle, fractioned
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Whole bunches go into the press, which works slowly and progressively, and the juice is split into cuvée and taille that are vinified separately; press centres need INAO approval (agrément simple or qualitatif)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: One 4,000 kg marc
slides.1.highlights.1.content: One marc is 4,000 kg of grapes giving at most 2,550 L: 2,050 L cuvée plus 500 L taille (Comité Champagne); the specification expresses it as at most 102 L per 160 kg
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Two characters of juice
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The specification says cuvée is rich in acidity and gives fresh, lively aromas, while taille is fruitier and richer in tannin
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Presses
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Traditional vertical basket presses (such as the Coquard type) remain common; the specification allows presses from 2,000 to 12,000 kg and limits the number of pressings a day
slides.1.content: Press fractions beyond 2,550 L are not AOC wine; they count as rebêche and must go for distillation.
slides.2.title: Settling and first fermentation
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Débourbage
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Juice must be settled before leaving the press centre, and 1–4% of the settled volume is removed as lees (bourbes)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Vessels and wood
slides.2.highlights.1.content: First fermentation is mostly in stainless steel, with some oak barrels; wood pieces such as chips are forbidden by the specification
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Malolactic fermentation
slides.2.highlights.2.content: MLF is optional (Comité Champagne): doing it gives a rounder wine, skipping it keeps malic acid and a sharper profile, and it is one of the style decisions
slides.2.highlights.3.title: A palette of separate wines
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Houses ferment varieties, villages, plots and press fractions separately, creating many base wines to blend from
slides.2.content: Base wines are usually high in acid, low in alcohol and not very pleasant; the magic comes from blending and time in bottle.
slides.3.title: Assemblage (blending)
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The heart of style
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Blends combine varieties, villages and years; the specification notes that Jules Guyot pointed out the importance of blending varieties and plots as early as 1866
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The goal of NV
slides.3.highlights.1.content: NV aims at a consistent house style: wines of the year bring freshness and vivacity, reserve wines add complexity and consistency (Comité Champagne)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Limits on Vintage
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Vintage wines use grapes of the year only (no reserve wine) and each operator may present no more than 80% of that year's wine as vintage
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Three ways to make rosé
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Direct pressing, maceration or saignée, or blending white and red wine before tirage; the red share is commonly 5–20% (Comité Champagne)
slides.3.content: D5 often asks how blending serves consistency, complexity and cost at once.
slides.4.title: Reserve wines
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The role of reserve wines
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Base wine kept from earlier years makes up for weaker vintages and keeps NV style stable; the specification says reserve wines bring riper, more evolved character to a blend
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The regulatory framework
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Cap of 10,000 kg of grapes per hectare per operator; extra yield may only fill the reserve and needs an individual request; reserve wines are quality-monitored and gain the AOC only on release, declared as if bottled
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Numbers in older articles
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Older articles quote a reserve cap of 8,000 kg/ha; the current INAO text says 10,000, which this course follows (and does not test)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Perpetual reserve
slides.4.highlights.3.content: A perpetual reserve (similar to a solera) is topped up with new wine each year while part is drawn off, giving a multi-vintage reserve; it is a house practice the specification does not specifically regulate
slides.4.content: Actual reserve shares differ by house, so no figure is given here.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which statement about cuvée and taille is correct?
A. Taille is the most acidic and freshest
B. Cuvée is higher in acidity and fresher; taille is fruitier with more tannin
D. Taille can only be distilled
The specification describes cuvée as acid-rich and lively and taille as fruitier and richer in tannin.
May a Vintage Champagne contain reserve wine?
B. Yes, but no more than 10%
C. No, it must come entirely from that year
A Vintage uses grapes of the year only, with no reserve wine, and is capped at 80% of the operator's wine of that year.
What is the INAO ceiling on an operator's reserve?
B. 12,400 kg of grapes per hectare
D. Each producer has a reserve ceiling (in kg of grapes per hectare)
12,400 is the base yield and 2,550 L is the juice per pressing; each producer also has a reserve ceiling in kg/ha (sources differ on the figure, so it is not tested).
